title: Measuring & Rulers
strapline: How long, how tall, how far — questions children can answer for themselves.
intent: Children explore length and height directly — comparing, ordering, and finding out what's longer, taller, shorter.
Children discover measuring as a way to answer real questions rather than an abstract skill.
Children use non-standard units first — cubes, footsteps, hands, string — and then meet rulers and tapes with meaning.
Children build the language of measure: long, longer, longest, tall, short, wide, deep, the same.
Children learn that fair measuring needs care — starting at the end, no gaps, no overlaps.
implementation: Put out tape measures, rulers, unifix cubes, lengths of string and a height chart, alongside things worth measuring.
Start from a real question: 'whose tower is tallest?' or 'will this ribbon reach across the table?'
Model measuring carefully — 'I start right at the end, no gaps' — and let children spot when it goes wrong.
Compare directly before measuring with units: hold two sticks side by side, line up two children back to back.
Record findings simply — a chart of 'how many cubes tall' each cuddly toy is, or footprints across the room.
Feed in comparative and superlative language constantly: longer than, the tallest, not as wide as.
Take measuring outdoors — how far can you jump, how deep is the puddle, how tall is the sunflower this week?
key_questions: Which one is longer — how could we find out for sure?
How many cubes tall do you think it is?
How can we measure fairly so it isn't cheating?
Whose is the tallest — how shall we put them in order?
How much has the plant grown since last week?

impact.text: Children compare and order objects by length and height.
Children measure using non-standard units, lining them up with care.
Children use the language of measure — long, tall, wide, deep, the same.
Children measure to answer a real question and share what they found.
Children begin to explore standard tools — rulers and tapes — with purpose.
Children persist to measure accurately and check their result.

enhancements: A growing chart on the wall where children can be measured each half-term.
A giant tape measure and trundle wheel for measuring the garden and corridors.
Ribbon, wool and string to cut 'as long as' a chosen object.
A collection of shoes and footprints to order from smallest to biggest.
Plant-growth measuring linked to the gardening area — a weekly cube count.
A builders'-yard prompt: cut the plank 'six cubes long' to fit the model.

playing_exploring: Children measure whatever fascinates them, from worms to their own arms.
Rulers and tapes are tools they explore freely before any task.
active_learning: Children keep measuring until it's fair and the answer feels right.
Answering their own question drives them to measure carefully.
creating_thinking: Children choose a way to measure and decide if it worked.
They predict which is longer, then test and compare their guess.
